claims.text: Current-dollar PCE increased $8.2 billion, a change described as 'less than 0.1 percent' (a less-than amount, not an exact percentage).

citations.quotation: personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased $8.2 billion (less than 0.1 percent).

claims.text: The current-dollar PCE increase reflected a $44.9 billion rise in services spending partly offset by a $36.7 billion decrease in goods spending.

citations.quotation: The $8.2 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in March reflected a $44.9 billion increase in spending for services that was partly offset by a $36.7 billion decrease in spending for goods (table 3).

claims.text: Personal saving was $1.00 trillion and the personal saving rate was 5.1 percent.

citations.quotation: Personal saving was $1.00 trillion in March and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of disposable personal income—was 5.1 percent (table 1).

claims.text: Real PCE decreased less than 0.1 percent (a less-than amount); real goods spending fell 0.4 percent while real services rose 0.1 percent.

citations.quotation: Real PCE decreased less than 0.1 percent; goods decreased 0.4 percent and services increased 0.1 percent (tables 5 and 7).

counterarguments.text: One might read the nominal PCE monthly change as exactly 0.1 percent, but the source explicitly labels it 'less than 0.1 percent,' so it should be reported as a less-than amount, unlike DPI (0.4 percent) which is exact. The revised February table, by contrast, lists exact figures (0.1 percent current-dollar, -0.2 percent chained) for February, not March.
